newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian govt parties see deal on tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Italian govt parties see deal on tax reform.

text.p: Parties which support Italy's centre-left government appeared on Wednesday to have reached a deal over controversial plans to reform the income tax system.
Key parties said after a meeting of parliamentary leaders of the pro-government bloc that the draft of the reform would be re-written by Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco and a senior parliamentarian.
"We have reached an accord," said Fabio Mussi, leader in the lower house of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), the biggest force in Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government.
The row broke out at the weekend when the hard left party Communist Refoundation voiced opposition to Finance Ministry plans to cut the number of tax brackets to five from eight.
The row had raised fresh uncertainty about passage of Italy's key 1997 budget, of which the fiscal reform is a part.

The hard left, which provides crucial external support to the government, complained that it had not been consulted and said it feared the changes would mean more tax for lower earners. Two meetings on Tuesday failed to deliver a deal.
"There is the basis for an accord," Oliviero Diliberto, the Communist Refoundation leader in the lower house, told reporters after Wednesday's talks.
He said the new text should "guarantee that fiscal pressure on the weaker groups will not increase by a single lira".

It was not immediately clear how the draft would be changed. It had envisaged raising the minimum income tax rate to 20 percent from 10 percent and cutting the maximum rate to 46 percent from 51 percent.
Apart from the income tax issue, the centrist Italian Renewal party, headed by Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, had also wanted plans for a new regional tax (IREP) to be dropped.
Mussi said further work was needed on the Irep issue though he and other politicians said an agreement had been reached that the regional tax proposal would be retained in some form.
